client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. I sit down to do my schoolwork but just end up staring at my laptop, thinking about her. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the pain feels too deep.
therapist:
I hear you describing deep pain about your grandma's passing, yet your voice sounds brighter than your words would suggest. I wonder if part of you is trying to push through this grief while another part feels overwhelmed by it?  

What comes up for you when you notice that tension between how you're describing your feelings and how you might actually be experiencing them right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I don't know...maybe I am trying to push through it. Everyone keeps telling me I should be "moving on" by now, but when I'm alone at night, it hits me so hard. I'll just be folding laundry and suddenly remember her hands showing me how to fold things properly, and then I can't breathe. 

But you're right - I do sound weirdly cheerful about it sometimes. I guess I'm scared if I really let myself feel it, I'll never stop crying. That sounds dramatic, but that's how it feels.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying this heavy grief while also feeling pressure to "move on," which leaves you caught between expressing your pain and holding it in.  

When you mention being scared you'll never stop crying if you let yourself feel it, I hear how overwhelming that fear is—would you be willing to explore what that "never stopping" might look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know...the idea of "never stopping" just feels like I'd drown in it. When I try to imagine letting the tears out completely, I picture myself collapsing and never being able to function again. Part of me thinks maybe I should just keep pushing through like I have been, even if it's exhausting.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding this fear that if you fully grieve, you'll lose control completely—that's such a painful thought to carry.  

I notice your words and voice both reflect that heaviness right now—would it feel safe to slow down for a moment and notice what happens when you let yourself just *be* with these feelings, without the pressure to push through?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know if I can just "be" with these feelings—that's exactly what scares me. Every time I start to really feel the loss, it's like I'm falling into a black hole and I panic. 

I guess part of me thinks if I let myself grieve completely, I'll never be able to pull myself back together again.
therapist:
Your fear of being consumed by grief makes so much sense—it sounds like you're worried that if you let yourself fall into these feelings, you won't be able to find your way back.  

I hear how overwhelming that feels right now—would it help to explore what "pulling yourself back together" might look like, even in small ways?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know if I can trust myself to "pull back together" once I start grieving. Last time I let myself really feel it, I couldn't get out of bed for days. What if that happens again but worse? 

The idea of doing it in small ways sounds better, but I'm not sure how to stop once I start. It feels like opening a floodgate that I can't control.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying this fear that grief will overwhelm you completely if you let it in, especially after that experience of not being able to get out of bed.  

What if we explored ways to dip your toes into these feelings—like testing the water—so you could practice noticing when to pause and when to let yourself feel? Would that feel safer than the idea of a floodgate?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying about testing the waters, but I'm scared even that small amount will pull me under. Last time I tried to let myself feel just a little, it's like my chest got crushed under this weight I couldn't lift. 

The floodgate metaphor is exactly how it feels - like if I open it even a crack, the whole thing will burst and I'll drown. I don't know how to trust that I can pause it once it starts.
therapist:
It sounds like even the idea of testing the waters feels overwhelming—like there's no safe way to approach these feelings without risking being pulled under.  

I hear how vivid that floodgate image is for you—what would it feel like to imagine yourself *with* those feelings, rather than being swept away by them? Could we explore that together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know if I can just sit with these feelings—they're so intense it's like they have a life of their own. When I try to imagine being with them instead of fighting them, I just feel this panic that I'll lose control completely. 

The floodgate image is exactly how it feels—like if I loosen my grip even a little, everything will come crashing through. I'm not sure I trust myself to handle that.
therapist:
I hear how terrifying it feels to loosen your grip even a little—like these emotions could completely overwhelm you if you stop fighting them.  

That panic about losing control makes so much sense—what if we tried imagining just *one small wave* at a time, rather than the whole flood? Would that feel any more manageable to explore?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about taking it one wave at a time, but honestly even that feels risky. Last time I tried easing up on controlling my anxiety, I had a full panic attack in the grocery store. It's like my brain screams that if I don't clamp down hard, everything will spiral.
therapist:
I hear how real that fear of spiraling is for you—especially after your experience in the grocery store, which sounds like it reinforced this belief that easing up leads to losing control.  

Your voice sounds quieter and flatter than usual as you describe this—what’s coming up for you right now as we talk about that memory?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I just feel so tired of this cycle. The grocery store incident keeps replaying in my head - how my chest got tight when I saw the crowded aisles, how I had to leave my cart and bolt for the door. Now I'm scared to even try going back there. 

Part of me thinks talking about it is pointless because the anxiety always wins anyway. Like my brain's wired wrong and I'll never get past this.
therapist:
It sounds like that grocery store experience left you feeling defeated—like no matter what you do, the anxiety takes over. I notice you're speaking more quietly than usual as you describe this—almost like you're exhausted from the fight.  

When you say your brain feels "wired wrong," I hear how hopeless that must feel—would you be willing to explore what "getting past this" might look like, even in a small way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, I guess I do feel exhausted. It's just... every time I think I'm getting better, something like this happens and I'm right back where I started. I don't even know what "getting past this" would look like anymore. 

The worst part is I know it's irrational - it's just a grocery store - but my body reacts like it's life or death. That's what makes me feel wired wrong. Like my own brain is working against me.
therapist:
I hear how frustrating it is to feel like you take steps forward only to be pulled back—it makes complete sense that you'd feel exhausted by that cycle.  

Even though you know the fear is irrational, your body reacts so strongly—that disconnect must feel so confusing. Would you be willing to explore what happens if we separate the idea of your brain being "wrong" from your brain being *protective*, even if it's overdoing it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
